method: Diffed the-capm-domain-by-domain-edition-layout.txt against edition-next.txt after stripping page numbers and running heads, then confirmed via a sorted bag-of-words comparison that the only differences are three de-duplicated table-header rows (each previously printed twice because its table split across a page break, now printed once) and a net increase in running-head/page-number furniture consistent with more total pages — net word-count delta zero, no vocabulary added or removed, and spot-checked the load-bearing content (72 seconds, 13 to 21, escalate/avoid, the Beck/Jacobson author lists, the Kanban six-practice list, the Domain 4 Task 4 answer key line) all present unchanged. Rendered the actual PDF at the given house path with pdftoppm (150dpi) for the page containing §6.6's "Roadmap." label (page 60) and its preceding page (59), and two further label-plus-table spots (§2.9's "A stakeholder register entry.", page 26; §5.7's "Requirements, classified.", page 53) to visually confirm each label now renders on the same page as its table. Diffed edition-num.txt against edition-layout.txt, then re-ran the diff after additionally stripping each line's leading section-number prefix (e.g. "0.1 ", "7.6 "): the word-bag comparison came back empty, confirming zero content differences beyond section numbers, page flow and the build hash. Confirmed by direct grep that all eight About-this-book headings, "Formulas", "Lists" and the four study-plan headings now print with no leading number anywhere in the text, while chapters 1–7's own numbered sections (spot-checked 1.1–1.12, 2.1–2.12, 7.1–7.5) are unaffected and still numbered. Diffed edition-final.txt against edition-num.txt directly (no normalization needed): only two lines changed, both stale running heads. Rendered the refreshed house PDF with pdftoppm at the odd pages carrying each affected running head (9 and 79) and confirmed the correct chapter titles now show, while confirming the other three named back-matter chapters (formulas and lists, study plan, references) are each too short to have a second odd page where the same bug could have appeared, so the two-line diff is the complete fix.

findings.claim: Chapter 3's "What you will be able to do" and body text cover Domain 2 Task 1's other three enablers but never restate or teach "Distinguish the differences between various project components."
findings.source: PMI, CAPM Examination Content Outline, 2023 Exam Update, Domain 2, Task 1 enablers (capm-eco-2023.pdf, p.8): "Distinguish the differences between various project components."
findings.fix: Verified fixed: a new §3.3 "The components of a predictive project" was added with a table distinguishing Charter, Project management plan, Subsidiary plans, Baselines, Phase, Deliverable, Work package, Activity and Milestone; §3.1's objectives now include "Distinguish a predictive project's components: the charter, the project management plan and its subsidiary plans, the baselines, phases, deliverables, work packages and milestones"; §3.11 Key terms lists the same set.

findings.claim: "up to three attempts within a one-year eligibility period" is the book's entire statement of the attempts rule, omitting the outline's 1-year wait-to-reapply after three failed attempts.
findings.source: capm-eco-2023.pdf, "Retaking the Exam" (pp.15–16): "After three attempts, you must wait 1 year from the date of your last examination before you can reapply for the certification."
findings.fix: Verified fixed: §0.3 now reads "up to three attempts within a one-year eligibility period; after three attempts without passing, you must wait a year from your last exam before reapplying," matching the outline's rule.

findings.claim: "Kanban practices: visualize, limit WIP, manage flow, make policies explicit, improve." under a header claiming "what the exam expects you to recall exactly" — five of Anderson's six core practices, omitting "implement feedback loops."
findings.source: David J. Anderson, Kanban: Successful Evolutionary Change for Your Technology Business (2010); the Kanban Method's six core practices: visualize the workflow, limit WIP, manage flow, make process policies explicit, implement feedback loops, improve collaboratively (evolve experimentally).
findings.fix: Verified fixed in this file: §7.7 now reads "Kanban practices: visualize, limit WIP, manage flow, make policies explicit, implement feedback loops, improve collaboratively" — all six items. Note: the same list in 04-agile-frameworks.md §4.7 was not updated to match; see new finding n1.

findings.claim: "Teams are grouped into an Agile Release Train that plans together in a regular, multi-week planning event and delivers on a shared cadence." mischaracterized PI Planning's own duration as multi-week.
findings.source: Scaled Agile, Inc., "PI Planning", framework.scaledagile.com/pi-planning: PI Planning is a two-day event held roughly every 8 to 12 weeks; the event itself is two days, not multi-week.
findings.fix: Verified fixed: §4.7 now reads "...plans together in a two-day planning event held every 8 to 12 weeks and delivers on a shared cadence."

findings.claim: The twelve PMBOK 7 principles were listed only as imperative one-line statements reproduced close to verbatim from the Standard, and the principles' own short names (Stewardship, Team, etc.) were never given anywhere in the book.
findings.source: PMI, PMBOK Guide, 7th ed. (2021): the twelve principles are named Stewardship, Team, Stakeholders, Value, Systems Thinking, Leadership, Tailoring, Quality, Complexity, Risk, Adaptability and Resiliency, and Change.
findings.fix: Verified fixed: §1.5 now numbers and names all twelve principles in PMI's official order ("1. Stewardship: care responsibly for the resources, people and trust placed in the project." ... "12. Change: enable the change that reaches the envisioned future state."), each with a paraphrase rather than a verbatim quotation; §1.10 Key terms and 08-formulas-and-lists.md §7.7 both now list the twelve names too. One statement (Change) still echoes the Standard's phrase "envisioned future state," but the set as a whole is a genuine paraphrase and the names are now present, which resolves the finding.

findings.claim: "a 20-week schedule baseline" for the Riverside project's plan, inconsistent with the 15-week critical path computed in the same running example in Chapter 3.
findings.source: 03-predictive-methods.md's critical-path network (activities A–G): "3 + 4 + 5 + 2 + 1 = 15 weeks."
findings.fix: Verified fixed: §2.9's worked example now reads "a 15-week schedule baseline," matching Chapter 3's 15-week critical path.

findings.claim: "A burnup chart shows total scope rising from 21 to 29 points when the language story is added" did not match the story-point table (5+3+2+3=13 before the language story; +8=21 after).
findings.source: Recomputed from the same section's story-point table.
findings.fix: Verified fixed: §4.9 now reads "A burnup chart shows total scope rising from 13 to 21 points when the language story is added," which matches the table (13 → 21).

findings.claim: Chapter 7 stated the exam's pace as "72 seconds a question" while the study plan's "On the day" section said "about 70 seconds a question" for the same figure.
findings.source: Recomputed from the outline: 3 hours ÷ 150 questions = 72 seconds a question exactly.
findings.fix: Verified fixed: both §7.1 and §7.11 "On the day" now say "72 seconds a question."

findings.claim: Three of the seven CAPM references named in §0.4 — Business Analysis for Practitioners, 2nd ed.; The Project Management Answer Book, 2nd ed.; and Effective Project Management, 8th ed. — had no bibliography entry.
findings.source: Internal: comparison of §0.4's prose against the back-matter References and against capm-eco-2023.pdf's own reference list (p.4).
findings.fix: Verified fixed: §0.4 now cites "(Project Management Institute 2024)" for Business Analysis for Practitioners, "(Furman 2015)" for The Project Management Answer Book, and "(Wysocki 2019)" for Effective Project Management; the References now include "Furman, Jeff. 2015. The Project Management Answer Book. 2nd ed. Management Concepts Press.", "Wysocki, Robert K. 2019. Effective Project Management: Traditional, Agile, Extreme, Hybrid. 8th ed. Wiley.", and "Project Management Institute. 2024. Business Analysis for Practitioners: A Practice Guide. 2nd ed." All three are real, correctly identified works matching the outline's own reference list.

findings.claim: Missing "author" fields on four bibliography entries (PMBOK 7, Process Groups: A Practice Guide, The PMI Guide to Business Analysis, Agile Practice Guide) caused their in-text citations to render with the full title doubling as author, producing redundant doubled-title parentheticals throughout the book.
findings.source: House style guide, §Conciseness; the four .bib entries themselves, which lacked an "author" field.
findings.fix: Verified fixed: all four entries (and the new Business Analysis for Practitioners entry) now carry "Project Management Institute" (or "Project Management Institute and Agile Alliance") as author, grouped with em-dash continuation in the References; every in-text citation now renders as a short "(Project Management Institute 2021)"-style parenthetical. Re-ran the original doubled-title search pattern against the new text: zero matches remain anywhere in the book.

findings.claim: The "self-awareness, self-regulation, motivation, empathy and social skill" formulation was attributed only to Goleman's 1995 book, though this exact five-label framing is more precisely from his 1998 HBR article "What Makes a Leader?"
findings.source: Daniel Goleman, "What Makes a Leader?", Harvard Business Review, 1998.
findings.fix: Verified fixed: §2.6 now cites "(Goleman 1995, 1998)", and the References add "Goleman, Daniel. 1998. \"What Makes a Leader?\" Harvard Business Review, 1998." alongside the existing 1995 entry.

findings.claim: "Threat responses: avoid, mitigate, transfer, accept." listed only four of PMI's five threat-response strategies, omitting "escalate."
findings.source: PMI's standard risk-response taxonomy: five threat strategies (avoid, mitigate, transfer, escalate, accept) and five opportunity strategies (exploit, enhance, share, escalate, accept); "escalate" applies to both threats and opportunities when the risk is outside the project's authority (confirmed by web search against current PMI/PMP teaching materials).
findings.fix: Verified fixed: §7.7 now reads "Threat responses: escalate, avoid, transfer, mitigate, accept. Opportunity responses: escalate, exploit, share, enhance, accept." — five items in each list, both correctly including "escalate."

findings.claim: Free float was defined in prose but never computed anywhere in the Riverside worked example, Check yourself questions, or Answers, unlike total float.
findings.source: 561 Group pedagogy note, "How a study companion should teach toward a credential" — constructive alignment.
findings.fix: Verified fixed and arithmetic re-checked: §3.10's worked example now computes "C's free float is E's early start minus C's early finish, 5 − 5 = 0" and "E's free float is F's early start minus E's early finish, 12 − 8 = 4" (both recomputed correct against the network's ES/EF/LS values). A new Check yourself Q8 ("In the Riverside network, what are C's total float and free float, and why do they differ?") and matching Answer 8 ("Total float 4 weeks; free float 0...") were added; the former Q8/A8 (customer formal acceptance) was correctly renumbered to Q9/A9 with its option list and answer letter (B) unchanged and still matched.

findings.claim: "Minimum viable product" was an uncited key term with no glossary entry, despite the evidence packet naming Ries (2011) as its source.
findings.source: 561 Group evidence packet, 2026-09-27-note-on-the-google-project-management-certificate-and-the-capm-exam.md.
findings.fix: Verified fixed: §6.2 now reads "...a minimum viable product, Eric Ries's term for the smallest version that delivers value and teaches the team what users want (Ries 2011)"; the References add "Ries, Eric. 2011. The Lean Startup. Crown Business."; and 10-glossary.md adds "Minimum viable product (MVP). The smallest version of a product that delivers value and teaches the team what users want. [6]".

findings.claim: §4.7's own Kanban paragraph — "Visualize the work on a board; limit work in progress per stage; manage flow; make policies explicit; improve continuously." — still lists only five of Anderson's six core Kanban practices, omitting "implement feedback loops." The f3 fix corrected the summary list in 08-formulas-and-lists.md but left this parallel description, the chapter's own teaching text, unchanged, so the book now states two different practice counts for the same method in two places.
findings.source: David J. Anderson, Kanban: Successful Evolutionary Change for Your Technology Business (2010), six core practices (as in f3); 08-formulas-and-lists.md §7.7, now corrected to six items, versus this paragraph's five.
findings.fix: Verified fixed: §4.7 now reads "Visualize the work on a board; limit work in progress per stage; manage flow; make policies explicit; implement feedback loops; improve collaboratively," matching the six-item list in 08-formulas-and-lists.md §7.7 exactly. (The SAFe paragraph immediately after it reflowed across the page break as a side effect; its text is unchanged and complete.)

findings.claim: The new §3.3 "The components of a predictive project" and §3.11 Key terms introduce Charter, Phase, Deliverable, Activity and Subsidiary plans as named concepts, but none of these gained an entry in 10-glossary.md, unlike Milestone, Baseline and WBS — terms of the same weight that already have entries. (Confirmed: the glossary runs directly from "Business case" to "Constraint" with no "Charter" entry, and has no "Phase," "Deliverable," "Activity" or "Subsidiary plan(s)" entries anywhere.)
findings.source: Internal: 03-predictive-methods.md §3.11 Key terms versus 10-glossary.md's alphabetical entries; the same "glossary vs. chapters" consistency check that produced the original f14 finding (which was fixed by adding a glossary entry).
findings.fix: Verified fixed: 10-glossary.md now has "Activity. A scheduled piece of work that produces part of a work package. [3]" (matches §3.3's table exactly); "Charter. The document that authorizes a project and names its project manager. [2, 3]" (agrees with §2.7's "The charter then authorizes the project and names the project manager" and §3.3's table); "Deliverable. A product, result or capability a project must produce. [3]" (matches §3.3); "Phase. A stretch of the life cycle ending in a major deliverable or decision. [1, 3]" (agrees with §1.4's simpler definition and §3.3's fuller one, correctly tagged to both); and "Subsidiary plan. A plan for managing one area of the project, such as scope, schedule, cost or risk. [2, 3]" (agrees with §2.2's subsidiary-plans table and §3.3). All five definitions and chapter tags agree with the chapters they cite. Placing the entries introduced a new ordering defect; see n3.

findings.claim: Two of the five glossary entries added to resolve n2 are out of the glossary's own alphabetical order: "Activity" is placed after "Agile Release Train" and before "Assumption" (it should be the second entry overall, right after "Acceptance criteria" and before "Adaptive life cycle"), and "Subsidiary plan" is placed before "Stakeholder register" (it should follow it, since "Sta-" sorts before "Sub-").
findings.source: Internal: the glossary's own established order (confirmed alphabetical for every other entry, including the other three new ones — Charter, Deliverable and Phase — which are correctly placed).
findings.fix: Verified fixed: re-read the full glossary in 10-glossary.md end to end. "Activity" now sits directly after "Acceptance criteria" and before "Adaptive life cycle." "Subsidiary plan" now sits directly after "Stakeholder register," and "Transition requirements" now sits between "Subsidiary plan" and "Tuckman's stages" (an ordering fault from the same earlier insertion that this pass also corrected, though it was not separately named in n3). Checked every consecutive pair in the glossary letter by letter: the full list is now strictly alphabetical from "Acceptance criteria" to "WBS; work package; WBS dictionary."

findings.claim: Two bibliography entries printed "et al." as though it were a literal second author's name, rather than a proper truncation of a real author list: "Beck, Kent, and et al. 2001." for the Agile Manifesto, and "Jacobson, Ivar, and et al. 1992." for the use-case book, both flagged by a sibling edition's proof and found to apply here too.
findings.source: agilemanifesto.org (fetched directly, front page and authors.html): the manifesto's seventeen signatories, in the site's own listed order, are Kent Beck, Mike Beedle, Arie van Bennekum, Alistair Cockburn, Ward Cunningham, Martin Fowler, James Grenning, Jim Highsmith, Andrew Hunt, Ron Jeffries, Jon Kern, Brian Marick, Robert C. Martin, Steve Mellor, Ken Schwaber, Jeff Sutherland and Dave Thomas. Independent catalog records (Amazon, Biblio, the ADS/Harvard abstract service) for Object-Oriented Software Engineering: A Use Case Driven Approach (1992) give its four authors as Ivar Jacobson, Magnus Christerson, Patrik Jonsson and Gunnar Övergaard. The Chicago Manual of Style's author-date rule for a source with more than ten authors is to list the first seven in the source's own order in the bibliography, followed by "et al."
findings.fix: Verified fixed: the References now read "Beck, Kent, Mike Beedle, Arie van Bennekum, Alistair Cockburn, Ward Cunningham, Martin Fowler, James Grenning, et al. 2001." — the first seven of the seventeen signatories, in agilemanifesto.org's own order, correctly truncated per the more-than-ten-authors rule (not "all seventeen" spelled out, but the standard, correct bibliographic form) — and "Jacobson, Ivar, Magnus Christerson, Patrik Jonsson, and Gunnar Övergaard. 1992.", all four real co-authors spelled out since there are fewer than ten. The in-text citations were also corrected, to "(Beck et al. 2001)" and "(Jacobson et al. 1992)". Grepped every remaining "et al." in the book (Cepeda et al. 2006, Dunlosky et al. 2013, Malcolm et al. 1959, plus these two): all are either ordinary in-text shorthand for a fully-spelled-out bibliography entry, or this one correct truncation. None is a literal "and et al." author-name bug.

findings.claim: In the PDF build, a bold label paragraph that introduces a table (e.g. "Roadmap.", "A stakeholder register entry.", "Requirements, classified.") could be stranded at the bottom of one page while its table started the next, most visibly in Chapter 6 where "Roadmap." previously ended a page with its table pushed to the following one.
findings.source: Coordinator's report of the previous PDF layout; house PDF build (LaTeX via pandoc).
findings.fix: Verified fixed: confirmed by diff that edition-layout's text differs from edition-next's only in page-break position and running-head/page-number furniture (a sorted bag-of-words comparison shows the sole content-level difference is three table-header rows that no longer print twice because their tables no longer split across a page — net word-count delta zero). Rendered the built PDF at /home/emsenn/info/lib/emsenn/services/561-group/services/561-group-services-section/data/state/editions/the-capm-domain-by-domain/the-capm-domain-by-domain.pdf with pdftoppm: page 60 now shows §6.6's "Roadmap." label immediately followed by its full three-row table (page 59 ends with only the §6.6 heading and blank space, pushed clear by the needspace filter rather than splitting the label from its table); page 26 shows §2.9's "A stakeholder register entry." label with its table intact on one page; page 53 shows §5.7's "Requirements, classified." label with its table intact on one page. The keep-with-table.lua filter with \usepackage{needspace} resolves the class of issue, not only the one cited example.

findings.claim: In PDF editions, sections belonging to an unnumbered chapter were numbered as though they continued the previous numbered chapter: the front matter printed its sections as "0.1 An independent companion" through "0.8 Who wrote it" (continuing backward from Chapter 1), and the study plan printed its sections as "7.8 The rule" through "7.11 On the day" (continuing forward from Chapter 7's "7.5 Answers"), with the formula sheet's "Formulas" and "Lists" likewise printed as "7.6" and "7.7".
findings.source: Another edition's proof, per the coordinator; confirmed independently in this book's own PDF/text output (the same defect pattern: 0.1–0.8, 7.6–7.11).
findings.fix: Verified fixed: diffed the-capm-domain-by-domain-edition-num.txt against edition-layout.txt directly, then re-diffed a version of each with every line's leading section-number prefix stripped — the resulting word-bag comparison is empty, so nothing besides section numbers, page flow and the build hash changed. Grepped the new text directly: all eight About-this-book headings ("An independent companion" through "Who wrote it"), "Formulas", "Lists", and all four study-plan headings ("The rule", "Six weeks to the exam", "With less time", "On the day") now print with no leading number anywhere in the file, and no stray "0.1"–"0.8" or "7.6"–"7.11" prefix remains. Spot-checked that chapters 1–7's own numbered sections are untouched: 1.1–1.12, 2.1–2.12 and 7.1–7.5 all still print with their correct numbers.

findings.claim: Pages within an unnumbered chapter (About, formulas and lists, study plan, glossary, references) carried the running head of the last numbered section reached, rather than the unnumbered chapter's own title: an odd page early in the About chapter showed "CONTENTS", and an odd page in the Glossary showed "7.5. ANSWERS" (Chapter 7's last numbered section, several chapters back).
findings.source: Another book's proof, per the coordinator; confirmed independently in this book's own text and rendered PDF.
findings.fix: Verified fixed: diffed the-capm-domain-by-domain-edition-final.txt against edition-num.txt — exactly two lines differ (plus the build hash, which happens to be unchanged this round since no manuscript bytes moved): the running head before §0.4's content changes from "CONTENTS" to "About this book", and the running head before the Glossary's "Process manager" entry changes from "7.5. ANSWERS" to "Glossary". Rendered the built PDF (same house path, refreshed) with pdftoppm: page 9 (odd, right-aligned running head) now reads "About this book"; page 79 (odd) now reads "Glossary"; even pages 8 and 78 correctly still carry the generic "The CAPM, Domain by Domain" head. Checked the other three named back-matter chapters (formulas and lists, pages 73–74; study plan, 75–76; references, 81–82): each is only two pages long, so its sole odd page is the chapter-opening page, which by this book's own house style never carries a running head (confirmed on pages 73, 75 and 81, all correctly blank above the chapter title) — there is no second odd page in those three chapters where a stale head could appear, so the two-line diff is the complete fix, not a partial one.
